What the figures show

Active attacks occur for a variety of reasons; sometimes they are planned and other times not. Here, we show the timing of active attacks from 2000 to 2025, a critical element for premeditated attacks with the goal of maximizing casualties. As the plots demonstrate, some dimensions of time are more informative than others.

By year There appear to be more events in the last five years (mean = 46) than the first five years (mean = 8) or second five years (mean = 13); however, this may be an artifact of media coverage. Attacks that occurred during the first part of this data collection period likely did not get the national coverage that they do now. Furthermore, technology and search engines have improved dramatically over the 26 years of this data collection period.

By month In contrast to the obvious upward trend in attacks across years, there appears to be only a modest trend related to months of the year. Active attacks tend to peak during the warmer months of the year (e.g., April through August account for 47.8% of attacks), though this trend is not a strong one. The relationship with temperature is similar to trends observed for certain types of violent crime (e.g., aggravated assault, homicide) that also tend to peak during the warmest parts of the year.

By day of the week Active attacks share no observable association with day of the week. This can be seen by the flat distribution of attacks across the week. So while there may be trends by year and month, attacks appear to be nearly equally likely on any given day of the week.

By hour of the day Active attacks tend to cluster around midday. While attacks that begin at midday exactly are relatively infrequent (only 3.9% of attacks), half of all attacks occur immediately before midday (8-11am hours account for 25.4% of attacks) or after midday (1-4pm hours account for 24.6% of attacks).

What the figures show

Many in the media attempt to create a profile describing the “average” attacker. The data do not support a profile beyond sex and number of attackers. Attackers were male 96.2% of the time. Furthermore, the attacker commits the attack alone 97.6% of the time. Beyond these characteristics, attackers are somewhat more varied.

Race and ethnicity Most attackers were either Caucasian (46.1%) or African American (29.3%). All other racial/ethnic groups (e.g., Latino, Asian, Middle Eastern) accounted for 21% of attackers, and race was unknown for 3.5%.

Age While the median age of attackers was 31 years old, attackers ranged in age from 12 to 88. Attackers in their twenties were the most plentiful group compared to any other decade of life. The age-trend of attackers adheres to the classic “age-crime curve” observed for nearly every crime type, peaking in late adolescence/early adulthood and steadily declining throughout the rest of the life course.

Weapon Active attacks can be carried out using any weapon though, in reality, only a very small minority of attacks (6.8%) were carried out using weapons other than firearms (e.g., knife, vehicle). Among firearms, pistols were the most common, used in 54.7% of all attacks, while rifles (e.g., AR15s) and shotguns were used in 29.2% and 8.4% of all attacks, respectively.

What the figures show

Defining where an attack occurred can be difficult. For instance, on January 8, 2011, a shooter attacked a meeting for U.S. Representative Gabrielle Giffords. This attack happened in the parking lot of a local Tucson grocery store. Had the attack happened in the store, it would have been classified as a business event; however, since the attack occurred in the parking lot it is coded as an outdoor event. Bear these fine distinctions in mind when examining the visualizations in this section.

Location type As seen here, the plurality of events happen at places of business (283 attacks; 44.6%). Places of business include retail locations, factories/warehouses, office space, and medical facilities (e.g., hospitals). Around a quarter of attacks (27.6%) happened in public (outdoor) spaces. Schools were attacked 85 times (13.4%). These events are aggregated and include attacks on all types of educational facilities, including K-12 and institutions of higher education. Lastly, 91 attacks (14.4%) happened at “Other” locations (e.g., houses of worship, government buildings, residences, and military bases).

Relationship to the location In a vast majority of attacks (65.5% of all attacks), the attacker(s) had no prior association with the attack location. For attackers with some relationship to the location, former/current employees (15.6%) and students (11.4%) were the most common relationship types, followed by indirect associations (6.5%; e.g., the attacker’s wife was associated with the location) and “other” associations (1.1%).

Relationship by location type When looking within location types, we find that most attackers had no relationship to the locations. Going beyond attackers with no relationship, we find some interesting patterns. Despite making up only 15.6% of attackers generally, attackers of businesses were current/former employees 29.7% of the time. A similar trend is observable in schools, though in this case, the vast majority of attackers were current/former students (83.5%). Only a small percentage of attacks on schools (11.8%) were perpetrated by an attacker with no relationship to the school.

Time of day by location type When grouped by location type, the tendency of attacks to occur around midday is still observable, though it is modest. The most noticeable trend can be seen with attacks at schools, where there is a strong tendency for attacks to occur during the morning hours prior to midday. Note: this plot shows the density of attacks within location types, meaning that the concentration of attacks is relative to other attacks within the same location type and not to concentrations displayed for other location types.

What the figures show

There were 4,287 casualties from active attacks between 2000 and 2025. Of these, 1,477 people died. The visualizations in this section examine the casualties of active attacks.

Attacks and casualties by year Attacks and total casualties (fatalities and wounded) have been increasing over the course of data collection (2000-2025). For specific years, however, there are noticeable spikes in the number of deaths. These spikes often correspond to some of the more well-known attacks. For example:

  • 2007: The attack on Apr. 16th at Virginia Tech, Virginia, resulted in 32 deaths, accounting for 47.1% of all deaths that year.
  • 2009: The attack on Nov. 5th at Fort Hood (now Fort Cavazos), Texas, resulted in 13 deaths, accounting for 20% of all deaths that year.
  • 2012: The school shooting on Dec. 14th at Sandy Hook Elementary School, Connecticut, resulted in 26 deaths, accounting for 29.2% of all deaths that year.
  • 2017: The attack on Oct. 1st in Las Vegas, Nevada, resulted in 58 deaths, accounting for 39.5% of all deaths that year.

Of note, while the number of active attacks did not decrease during the COVID-19 pandemic, the lethality of attacks in 2020 decreased to less than half the number of any of the four years previous. In 2021, however, the number of attacks increased and the number of deaths returned to pre-pandemic levels.

Wounded and killed per attack Most attacks (85.6%) resulted in fewer than 10 casualties (killed and/or wounded) and 33% of attacks resulted in no deaths at all. Hover over the points on this plot to get information about that specific attack. Note: hovering over a point on one side of the plot will highlight a corresponding point on the other side.

Wounded and killed by weapon Most attacks (54.7% of all attacks) were committed using pistols. Among these, total fatalities were generally less than 20 (except for the attack at Virginia Tech, 2007). Similarly, nearly all pistol attacks resulted in <20 wounded (except the attack at Fort Hood, 2009). Rifle attacks accounted for 6 of the 7 attacks that surpassed 20 deaths. However, a mix of vehicle and rifle attacks accounted for nearly all attacks with more than 20 wounded. Hover over the points on this plot to get information about that specific attack.

What the figures show

Active attacks have been recorded in 49 states and the District of Columbia. The only state with no recorded attacks is Delaware. While most states have at least some number of attacks, the number of attacks (and fatalities) tends to cluster geographically. The visualizations in this section show that geographic dimension.

Attacks and fatalities by state The number of active attacks in a state strongly corresponds to the number of fatalities; however, there are some cases where the relative numbers of attacks and fatalities might not align. This map shows how states stack up to one another regarding the raw number of attacks and fatalities. Hover over the map to get information about specific states or over the legend to see which states are grouped together. Tip: click states or legend tiles to freeze selections to make comparisons with other states/groups.

Attacks by year (animation) The number of attacks and fatalities has risen over the period. This animation shows the location, primary weapon, and number of fatalities (<4, 4+) of each attack, year by year from 2000 to 2025.

Reading these numbers

Columns. The first column covers every attack in the data, with its share of the total (firearm types are a share of firearm attacks). The 2025 column is a count, and vs. 2024 is the change from the year before (2024 counts are in the PDF). Single years hold few attacks, so a change of a few events is within normal year-to-year variation; the five-year average gives the longer view.

Definitions. One weapon includes vehicle attacks and attacks with a firearm of unknown type. Race counts every attacker (unknown included), so its rows total the number of attackers, not attacks. Shot by civilian includes off-duty officers and security guards. Fled the scene includes a small number of attackers who fled after police arrived. Victim counts follow ALERRT’s definitions, which are stricter than the FBI’s (see Download the Data). Year-by-year figures always come from the current version of the data, so attacks identified later are counted in the year they happened.

About the data

The Research Ring at ALERRT makes the Active Attack Data freely available. Browse it here, or download the full dataset as a CSV file. The codebook lists every variable with its label, values, and missing counts, on its own page and as a PDF.

One row per attack Each of the 634 rows is one active attack, from 2000 through 2025. The 46 variables cover when and where it happened, the attackers and their weapons, the people shot, wounded, and killed, and how it ended.

Attacker variables Because some attacks involved more than one attacker, age, sex, and race carry a suffix for each attacker (age_1, age_2, age_3). For an attack with one attacker, the _2 and _3 variables are empty. The order is arbitrary: attacker 1 was not more central to the attack than the others.

Inclusive counts Variables ending in _incl use the FBI’s more inclusive definition. ALERRT counts only people shot, wounded, or killed by the attacker, so an injury suffered while fleeing is not in wound_tot. Where our figures differ from the FBI’s annual reports, this is usually why.

How attacks ended resolution records how each attack ended, and resolved_pre_le whether that happened before law enforcement arrived. The few attackers who fled after police arrived are counted with those who fled before, since nearly all fleeing attackers leave before police reach the scene.

Versions Version 2025 was released September 8, 2026; the relationship coding was corrected November 6, 2026. Every change is listed under Updates on the Home page. Earlier versions are kept for reproducing earlier work: v2024 data and codebook; v2023 data and codebook.

Using the data Please cite the data when you use them. Suggested citation:

Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training (ALERRT) Center. (2026). Active Attack Data (Version 2025) [Data set]. Texas State University. https://activeattackdata.org

A BibTeX entry is on the codebook page. Questions and corrections: Contact.

Related datasets Two datasets built from these data, K-12 door security and officers shot, are on the More Data page.
